name: Bilal Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer at Harbour & Vine Provisions, which supplies coffee, tea, spices and dry goods to independent cafes and small grocers. My mornings are video calls with growers and cooperatives, often early because of time zones, and then I check which shipments are stuck at port. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise long supplier emails and to translate when my Portuguese isn't up to a contract clause. Afternoons I taste samples and argue about price, and that's honestly my favourite part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The wearing part is the price swings, because a frost in one region can wreck a quarter's margins. I like that I can point to a cafe in town and say, I chose that coffee. My partner Inês teaches at a secondary school, so our weekends are marking piles and long lunches, and it's a calm life that I don't take for granted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in small doses and overhyped as a revolution. At work I'd keep using it for summaries and translations and tell the team it's a decent assistant, nothing more. Online I'd probably stay quiet, because I don't want to join an argument I can't win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm quite relaxed. My job runs on trust with growers and a good palate, and neither moves because of a chatbot. My worries are the ordinary ones: coffee prices, currency swings and whether Harbour & Vine keeps its biggest cafe customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do, and use the tool a little more where it's proven, like drafting purchase confirmations. I'd keep saving about a quarter of my pay and keep my emergency fund at around eight months. Inês and I would go on planning a trip to visit a cooperative in the highlands next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already live in, with its usual stress around prices and shipping, and I'm fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the biggest cafe customers. What would worry you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One chain of nine cafes takes nearly a fifth of our coffee. If they switched supplier, I'd be in a room explaining it to my boss, even if the cause was nothing I did. So I work hard to keep that relationship warm, with visits and tastings rather than discounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you rely on the tool you use now and then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than people assume. I'd say five percent of my week. It saves me an hour of reading, but I always check the numbers myself, because one wrong figure in a contract can cost real money.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent assistant**, not a revolution.
At work I'd tell the team to keep using it for **summaries** and translations.
Online I'd stay quiet, since I can't win that **argument**.
think: Privately I'm **relaxed**, because my job runs on trust with growers and a good palate.
My real worries are **coffee prices** and losing our biggest cafe customer.
do: I'd use the tool a bit more for **purchase confirmations**, where it's proven.
I'd keep saving a **quarter** of my pay and an eight-month fund.
I'd plan a visit to a **cooperative** with Inês next year.
feel: I feel **calm**, since this is the world I already live in.
S0.quote: My job runs on trust with growers and a good palate, and neither moves because of a chatbot.
fieldNote: He is secure here; his only live worry is **customer concentration** at one cafe chain.
He uses AI for about **five percent** of his week and checks numbers himself.
He cares about **growers** as people, a thread that returns in later answers.

steps.text: Use the tool to draft purchase confirmations once checked
Keep saving a quarter of pay and the eight-month fund
Carry on with grower calls and Friday sample tastings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be honest about which tasks the software takes and which stay with people. I'd tell friends it's a big shift, not a catastrophe, and that the speed depends on the rules we set. Online I'd say governments should fund retraining before the cuts, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is on the card by name, so I'd expect our team of five to be asked to do the same work with fewer people. I'm senior, so I'd probably be the one running the software rather than losing my job. But I can see the junior roles, like order entry and checking invoices, going first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead by learning the company's new buying system properly and offering to run the pilot, since being the person who understands it is the safest place to stand. I'd move more of my time to growers and relationships, which software handles badly. I'd keep my savings steady and put some into a broad index fund, because I'd rather have a cushion that grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit excited. I don't think the job disappears, but it changes shape, and I don't know if I'll like the new shape as much as the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said junior roles go first. Who would you think of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateus, who started last year and handles the invoice checking. He's quick, and I'd want to show him how to supervise the software rather than compete with it. I'd feel bad if we trained him and then let him go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up if the new shape wasn't to your taste?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give up the title before I gave up the tasting and the grower calls. If the job turned into watching dashboards all day, I'd look at moving into sourcing at a roaster or a fair-trade body, where the work is still about people.

say: I'd say we must be **honest** about which tasks software takes and which stay with people.
I'd tell friends it's a big shift, **not a catastrophe**.
Online I'd say governments should fund **retraining** before the cuts.
think: Our buying team of five will probably do the same work with **fewer people**.
I'm senior, so I'd likely **run the software**, while junior roles go first.
do: I'd learn the new buying system properly and offer to **run the pilot**.
I'd spend more time with **growers**, which software handles badly.
I'd put some savings into a broad **index fund** so the cushion grows.
feel: I feel **uneasy** and a little excited, unsure I'll like the new shape of the job.
S1.quote: I'd give up the title before I gave up the tasting and the grower calls.
fieldNote: He plans to become the **person who understands** the software, which fits his steady style.
His worry centres on **Mateus**, a junior colleague, and on training someone to lose a job.
He has a clear **fallback**: sourcing at a roaster or fair-trade body.

steps.text: Offer to run the pilot of the new buying system
Put part of savings into a broad index fund
Keep the grower calls and tastings as my core work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast, and we need a basic safety net and proper notice rules now. At work I'd push the company to be open about what's planned. Online I'd argue that growers and small cafes also need protection, not only office workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd expect my role to be mostly done by software within two years, since everything on my screen is thinking work. Cafes would still want coffee, and growers still need paying, but the sourcing could be done by a system. Robots matter little for me, but the thinking part arrives first, so I don't get the three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop planning trips and a deposit on a flat, and add to my emergency fund until it's a year's worth. I'd talk to Inês about whether she could take extra tutoring, since teaching is hands-on and slower to change. And I'd start talking to people at roasters and trading houses now, to find which jobs still need a human who knows growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I've got savings and a partner with a steady job, so I'd feel the shock but not the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Inês the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're lucky to have a cushion and we should treat it as a bridge, not a treat. Then I'd ask her honestly how she feels about our plans, because mine would be shaken more than hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the AI tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than before, since refusing wouldn't change anything. If the system will do my job, I'd rather be the person who knows how to direct it, and who knows the growers, than someone who just watched it happen.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and we need a safety net and proper notice rules.
I'd press the company to be **open** about what it plans.
I'd argue that **growers** and small cafes need protection too.
think: I'd expect software to do most of my **sourcing** within two years, since it's all screen work.
Robots matter little for me, but thinking AI arrives first, so I get **no extra time**.
do: I'd stop planning trips and a **flat deposit** and grow the fund to a year.
I'd ask Inês about extra **tutoring**, since teaching changes more slowly.
I'd start talking to **roasters** and trading houses about jobs needing someone who knows growers.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but not frozen, with savings and a steady partner.
S2.quote: If the system will do my job, I'd rather be the person who knows how to direct it, and who knows the growers
fieldNote: He expects the **thinking** part of his job to go on the stated date.
The household cushion and Inês's teaching job keep him **anxious**, not panicked.
He turns to **networking** with roasters early, a sign of steady adaptability.

steps.text: Grow the emergency fund to a full year of costs
Drop the trip and the flat deposit plans
Meet roasters and trading houses about people-based sourcing jobs
Practise directing the AI tool on real buying work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a real window, and we should use it to rewrite what training and unemployment support look like. At work I'd suggest we plan the buying team's future in public. With friends I'd say plan, but don't rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like a long runway, but I'd still expect my current role to disappear around then. I'd be 32, with a master's and experience, so I think I'd land somewhere. The worry is that everyone else would also be looking at the same moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to move toward growers and the origin side, maybe spending time with a cooperative and getting qualified in sourcing standards. I'd keep saving, and I'd buy a small flat with Inês, since five years is enough to make it work. I'd also keep using AI tools to stay current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. There's an edge of worry, but five years gives room to choose rather than react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone would be looking at the same moment. How would you stand out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being where the human trust sits. A buyer who has spent years in the field with a cooperative, who speaks the language and has been to the farms, is much harder to replace than someone who ran a screen. I'd start building that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a flat sounds like a big commitment. Why that choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with a strong cushion it gives us a base, and housing is the one cost that doesn't go to software. If our jobs change, a mortgage we can carry is better than rent that can rise.

I'd suggest we plan the buying team's future **in public**.
With friends I'd say **plan, but don't rush**.

I'd be 32 with a master's, so I think I'd **land somewhere**.
do: I'd spend time at a **cooperative** and qualify in sourcing standards.
I'd buy a small **flat** with Inês, since our cushion can carry the mortgage.
I'd keep using **AI tools** to stay current.
feel: I feel **fairly steady**, with five years giving room to choose rather than react.
S3.quote: A buyer who has spent years in the field with a cooperative, who speaks the language and has been to the farms, is much harder to replace
fieldNote: He plans to move to the **origin side**, where trust is hardest to automate.
The flat is a **hedge**: a mortgage he can carry beats rent that can rise.
His main worry is **competition** for the same fallback jobs.

steps.text: Spend a month at a growers' cooperative learning the origin side
Buy a small flat with Inês within two years
Keep using AI tools on the weekly buying plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like a gift, as long as we use it. I'd say at work we should treat it like a long change programme with clear steps, and I'd tell friends to keep learning. Online I'd push for strong public education budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty calm, because a decade is a long time and I'd be 37, still mid-career with options. My main fear would be doing nothing for years because it feels distant. I'd probably still find a role connecting growers and buyers, or move into a fair-trade body.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job, keep learning the AI tools as they improve, and keep buying skills fresh. I'd save, buy the flat, and maybe start a small side business importing one single-origin coffee with a friend. I'd also think about starting a family with Inês, since ten years gives us time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with some curiosity. I'd treat it like a slow tide I can watch rather than a wave about to hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a side business. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One coffee from one cooperative, sold to a few cafes I already know. It would start small, on weekends, and it would teach me the other side of trading. If the big jobs shrink, I'd have a small thing of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the decade change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make me more willing, to be honest. With ten years of notice I'd rather start a family with Inês at around thirty and keep our jobs flexible than put off the biggest life choice because of a headline.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if we use it well.
At work I'd treat it like a **long programme** with clear steps.
Online I'd push for strong **public education** budgets.
think: I'm **calm**, since at 37 I'd still be mid-career with options.
My real risk is **doing nothing** because the change feels distant.
do: I'd keep learning **AI tools** as they improve and keep my buying skills fresh.
I'd start a small **side business** importing one single-origin coffee with a friend.
I'd plan to **start a family** with Inês around thirty.
feel: I feel **mostly calm** and curious, like watching a slow tide.
S4.quote: One coffee from one cooperative, sold to a few cafes I already know.
fieldNote: Ten years turns the scenario into a **planning** exercise rather than a threat.
The side business is a **small hedge** that also teaches him the other side of trading.
Family plans are **freed** by the long notice.

steps.text: Keep up with new AI buying tools each quarter
Import one single-origin coffee on weekends with a friend
Plan to start a family with Inês around thirty
Keep saving a quarter of pay for the flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because buying is almost exactly what the card says goes first. What would help is a decent public safety net and some proper notice from employers, so people aren't just dropped. Also, honest conversations between companies and staff, because the worst version is everyone pretending nothing is happening.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who benefits. People talk about jobs but not about the growers, who are the people I actually think about. If software squeezes prices to the bone, a farmer in the highlands is the one who pays, and I'd want rules about that too.

He expects the thinking part of buying to go first, so he moves toward **growers** and the origin side.
He worries about junior colleague **Mateus** and about growers squeezed by software-driven prices.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, since buying is what the card says goes first.
